pass_a_gloss: Boasting in works of the law is excluded; Paul says, 'May I never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.' He insists he will not boast except in the cross alone. We conclude that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. The law of faith suffices for justification even for those who have done no works. We prove this with the thief on the cross and the sinful woman who anointed Jesus’ feet, whose sins were forgiven not by works but by faith, and who heard, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.' After knowing the truth, sin undermines grace, as Paul will show. He thinks that even pre-faith works, if they seem right, do not justify if not built on faith. Is God the God of Jews only? No, also of Gentiles, since one God justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. What advantage then has the circumcised who is justified by faith over the uncircumcised justified through faith? Not that Paul used his privileges differently. As when the wife says she is from the husband and the husband through the wife—she comes from him first, not through him; he comes from ancestors first, then through her. So circumcision is more noble, and the uncircumcised seeks justification through faith to be justified, not having come from faith; but the believer comes to circumcision, especially the hidden one Paul mentions, so it is better to be justified by faith than through faith, as being from a man is better than being through a woman. Concerning the Savior, it is not said he came through a woman, for though all men come through women after coming from men, the Savior did not come from a man, so he came from a woman but not through her. Do we then nullify the law by faith? May it never be! We uphold the law. Why did he not say 'by faith' but 'through faith'? The one justified by faith is circumcision; if the law were nullified by faith, then circumcision justified by faith would be nullified; but the uncircumcised justified through faith nullifies the law. Yet we received the Mosaic law through faith, not nullified, for faith establishes the law as from God. This is clear when speaking of true faith. If someone objects from 2 Corinthians about the ministry of death in letters being glorious, so that Israelites could not look at Moses’ face because of the glory, we say: Is it that the law is nullified, or that we nullify the law? Paul does not nullify the law; if it is nullified, it is by the surpassing glory of Christ, of whom it is said he is Lord of the Sabbath, and the fading glory was not glorified in comparison to the surpassing glory. The enduring he named Christ’s; the fading, the law nullified, since the law is a guardian until the fullness of time. If Abraham were justified by works, he would have something to boast, but not before God. For what does the Scripture say?
pass_b_english: Boasting in legal observance has no place; Paul declares, 'Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.' He affirms that he will glory in nothing else. Thus we conclude that a person is justified by faith, independent of works of the law. The law of faith is sufficient for justification, even for those who have done nothing. We demonstrate this through the thief on the cross and the woman who anointed Jesus’ feet with perfume, whose sins were forgiven not by deeds but by faith, and to whom he said, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace' [[Romans >> Bible:Romans 3:28]]. After coming to know the truth, sin destroys grace, as Paul will later make clear. He also maintains that even works done before faith, if they appear commendable, do not justify unless grounded in faith. Is God the God of Jews alone? Certainly not; he is also God of the Gentiles, since there is one God who justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. What advantage then does the circumcised person justified by faith have over the uncircumcised justified through faith? Not that Paul exercised his privileges differently. Just as a wife says she comes from her husband and the husband says he comes through his wife—she originates from him first, not through him; he originates from his ancestors first, then through her—so circumcision holds a position of priority, and the uncircumcised seeks justification through faith to be justified, not having originated from faith; but the believer approaches circumcision, especially the hidden kind Paul refers to, making justification by faith superior to justification through faith, just as being from a man is preferable to being through a woman. Regarding the Savior, it is not said that he came through a woman, for although all people come through women after coming from men, the Savior did not come from a man, so he came from a woman but not through her. Do we then abolish the law by faith? Certainly not! We uphold the law. Why did he say 'through faith' rather than 'by faith'? The one justified by faith is circumcision; if the law were annulled by faith, then circumcision justified by faith would be annulled; but the uncircumcised justified through faith would annul the law. Yet we received the Mosaic law through faith, not annulled, for faith establishes the law as originating from God. This is evident when speaking of genuine faith. If someone objects from 2 Corinthians about the ministry of death inscribed in stone being glorious, so that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its radiance, we ask: Is it that the law is annulled, or that we annul the law? Paul does not annul the law; if it is annulled, it is by the surpassing glory of Christ, of whom it is said he is Lord of the Sabbath, and the fading glory was not glorified in comparison to the surpassing glory. The enduring he named Christ’s; the fading, the law annulled, since the law serves as a guardian until the fullness of time. If Abraham had been justified by works, he would have had something to boast about—but not before God. For what does the Scripture say? He believed, and it was credited to him as righteousness [[Romans >> Bible:Romans 4:3]].

bible_refs.note: Paul's declaration about boasting only in the cross (Galatians 6:14) and justification by faith apart from works (Romans 3:28) are central to the argument.
The forgiveness of the sinful woman and the thief on the cross illustrates justification by faith apart from works (Luke 7:36-50; Luke 23:39-43).
The question of God's justice for Jews and Gentiles alike, and the role of faith in justification (Romans 3:29-30).
The analogy of coming from vs. through, applied to circumcision and faith, to show priority of origin (Romans 4:1-12).
Christ as Lord of the Sabbath and the surpassing glory that does not abolish but upholds the law (Matthew 12:8; 2 Corinthians 3:7-11).
Abraham's justification by faith, not works, as the foundation of God's promise (Romans 4:1-5; Genesis 15:6).
Paul's boast only in the cross of Christ
Justified by faith apart from works of the law
The sinful woman who anointed Jesus' feet
